newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ wants house asset costs out of CPI.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ wants house asset costs out of CPI.

text.p: Housing asset costs and interest rate movements should be excluded from measurement of the Consumer Price Index, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said in a submission to the national CPI Revision Advisory Committee.

The current measurement of housing costs in the CPI reflected the costs of the assets, including land and buildings, that provide shelter, not just currently, but over many periods, the bank wrote in its submission, published on Friday.

"A more appropriate basis for measuring the cost of current consumption of shelter is to adjopt a rental equivalence approach," it said, adding that that was the approach adopted by most OECD countries.
Such an approach could be done at reasonable cost and "would not involve a more significant 'abstraction' from true market prices than is the case with the currrent methodology", it said.
A five-yearly review of the CPI index is underway and the RBNZ has one member on an advisory committee which has been meeting to make recommendations on changes to the index.
"We do not believe that interest rates should be included in the CPI as they do not represent consumption in the traditional sense," the bank said.
People did not consume debt and therefore an interest rate was not a price, it said. It recommended that the concept underlying the CPI should be based on a consumption approach.
There are two methods widely used to calculate CPIs. One is consumption-based, which measures the value of goods and services consumed in a given of period regardless of price paid.
The treatment of housing costs has been a major sticking point within the committee, according to media reports.

A report prepared for the bank by Steven Bourassa of the Auckland University Property Department said the current method for measuring housing costs in New Zealand was "at best only distantly related to what the CPI should be measuring."
Bourassa recalculated the CPI from 1990-96 using imputed rentals and found that the index was much less volatile than the current method based on user costs.
As it has previously indicated, the bank said it was convinced interest rates did not belong in the CPI.
The other is the expenditure-based approach, favoured by Statistics New Zealand (SNZ), which measures the price of goods and services regardless of whether they are consumed or not.

Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said in a preface that the bank's submission was aimed at encouraging a CPI that was clear in terms of what it aimed to measure and how best that could be translated into reality.
The submission was not aimed at the narrow perspective of what might be useful for the purposes of monetary policy.
He said the various purposes for which the CPI could be used were not mutually exclusive or incompatible.
"In the bank's view, a good clear conceptual basis for the construction of the CPI is an essential starting point, if not the end point, for all its potential uses," Brash said.
The bank also highlighted local authority rates as an area which needed review -- arguing that rates were not an accurate measure of the price of services.
Services provided by local authorities were bundled and therefore changes in their price were difficult to measure because changes in quality and quantity also had to be considered.
However, the Reserve Bank stopped short of recommending that local authority rates should be removed from the CPI.
